items.phrase: Who cooks, for you; who cooks for you-all
items.grounds: The eight low arched notes, grouped as a pickup, a pair, two singles and a closing pair, with the drawn-out falling slur at the end, gave me eight beats with a long falling last syllable; but the words themselves came from the well-known Barred Owl mnemonic 'who cooks for you, who cooks for you all', which I already knew, and I fitted it to the count rather than finding it in the picture.
items.elements: Low hoots around 0.5 kHz, each with arched harmonics stacked up to about 2 kHz: a faint lone note at 0.3 s, then arched hoots at about 0.8, 1.15, 1.4, 1.9, 2.4, 2.8 and 3.05 s, the last one trailing off in a long downward slur that ends around 3.6 s. The hoots come in loose groups: one, a pair, one, one, then a pair that ends in the slur.

items.phrase: Ohhh, sweet, dear, home
items.grounds: One long held high tone followed by three level notes, each a step lower than the last, with the final one held, gave me a long opening vowel and three falling one-syllable words with the last one drawn out; I knew the 'Old Sam Peabody' and 'O sweet Canada' mnemonics, but this cut has no triplets, so I did not use them, though 'sweet' probably came from that memory.
items.elements: Clear pure whistles: one long, steady, very slightly falling tone at about 4.4 kHz from 0 to 2 s, then three shorter steady tones that step down, at about 4.5 kHz (2.3 to 2.9 s), about 4.0 kHz (3.1 to 3.6 s) and about 3.2 kHz (3.8 to 4.9 s, the longest of the three). Fainter chips and short sweeps from another bird sit behind them at 2 to 6 kHz.

items.phrase: Hi, there
items.grounds: Two pure tones, the first higher and slightly falling and the second lower, level and longer, suggested a two-word greeting with the pitch dropping onto a held second word; I already knew the 'fee-bee' and 'hey, sweetie' renderings of this song, and that knowledge surely nudged me toward a greeting.
items.elements: Two clean whistled notes: a first note at about 3.9 kHz drifting down to 3.6 kHz (0.25 to 0.63 s), a short gap, then a lower and slightly longer note held level at about 3.1 to 3.2 kHz (0.73 to 1.2 s), with a faint tail.

items.phrase: Wee wee, slide down, tick tick tick tick tick tick, DROP DROP DROP DROP, up
items.grounds: The groups in the picture set the words: two rising notes, two falling notes, six small quick ones, four loud steep falls, and one last rise, so each word covers one element and the stress falls on the loud final four; I knew the 'sweet sweet sweet, I'm so sweet' mnemonic, but it did not fit this count and I did not use it.
items.elements: A fast run of short slurred notes: two upslurs climbing to about 8 kHz (0.1 and 0.3 s), two downslurs from about 7 kHz (0.47 and 0.62 s), six small quick notes with a down-up shape around 3 to 5 kHz (about 0.75 to 1.5 s), then four loud, wide downstrokes from about 7 kHz to 4 kHz (1.65 to 2.17 s), and a final rising stroke (about 2.27 s).

items.phrase: Snap! Rise-up, burr, down, quick, ping, drop
items.grounds: Each word copies the shape of one element: a hard click at the start, a long climb with a hook, a buzzy burst, a falling slur, a quick up-and-down, a high snap and a final drop; I knew the 'quick, give me a rain check' / 'pick-up-a-real-chick' mnemonics for this species, but I did not use them, since the words here come from the shapes.
items.elements: A varied, choppy phrase: a sharp broadband chip at 0.27 s, a long smooth rise from 2 to 4.5 kHz (0.5 to 0.72 s) ending in a short down-hook, a burst of buzzy broadband pulses (about 0.9 to 1.05 s), a falling slur from 3 to 2 kHz (1.07 to 1.2 s), a quick up-and-down stroke (about 1.3 s), a very sharp high upsweep to about 10 kHz (1.5 s), and a final short downstroke (1.57 s).

items.phrase: Oh, pick pick pick pick pick, see-shiverrrr
items.grounds: The long opening note became a drawn-out 'Oh', the five identical short chips became five 'pick's, and the falling slur into a flat pulsing trill became 'see' falling into a rolled 'shiver'. None of the words came from the familiar 'drink-your-tea' mnemonic, though I know it, and this cut does not match it well because it has five chips instead of one or two.
items.elements: One longer, slightly falling opening note around 3-4 kHz (0.27-0.5 s). Then five short, evenly spaced, sharp hooked chips at about 3.7 kHz (0.62-1.15 s). Then a steep down-slur from about 8 to 5 kHz that runs straight into a long, flat, buzzy trill at about 4.7 kHz with roughly 11 pulses (1.3-1.78 s).

items.phrase: Peter Peter Peter Peter Peter Peter Peter Peter Peter
items.grounds: Each unit is two strokes, a high, light first one and a lower, heavier falling second one, so I used a two-syllable word stressed on the first syllable, nine times, getting louder. The word choice and the stress pattern were influenced by the 'teacher, teacher' mnemonic I already knew for this species.
items.elements: Nine repeated two-part units, about 0.3 s apart, that grow louder through the song. Each unit is a thin high stroke at about 4.6-6 kHz followed by a hooked down-sweep to about 3 kHz. A faint lower falling note ends the song at about 2.9 s.

items.phrase: tip tip tip tip tip, TIP, why? why? DOWN
items.grounds: The five matching short notes became 'tip' repeated, the single higher note became a stressed 'TIP', the two upward sweeps became the question 'why?' twice, and the big final fall became an emphatic 'DOWN'. I deliberately avoided the 'pleased to meet you' mnemonic I know, but knowing it probably made me notice the strong accented ending.
items.elements: Five short notes in a row, each rising sharply to about 6.5 kHz and then dropping to about 5 kHz (0.22-0.98 s). Then one higher note falling from about 9 to 6 kHz (1.07 s). Then two notes sweeping up from about 3 to 6.5 kHz (1.15-1.55 s), and a final loud, long down-slur from about 9 to 3 kHz (1.6-1.75 s).

items.phrase: fizz, BEER, oh
items.grounds: The buzzy flat note became 'fizz', the loud high upsweep became the stressed 'BEER', and the short drop became 'oh'. 'BEER' came from the 'free beer' mnemonic I already knew, not only from the picture.
items.elements: The main singer starts at about 1.3 s with a flat, rough, buzzy note at about 3.5 kHz. Next comes a sharp upward sweep that reaches 5-10 kHz (1.62-1.75 s), then a short falling note to end (1.78-1.83 s). Two fainter phrases, each a rise then a fall, come before it (0-1.05 s) and look like a different or more distant bird.

items.phrase: Whyyy? Whyyy? here, here, here, here, here
items.grounds: The two long rising sounds read as drawn-out questions, 'Whyyy?', and the five quick falling notes became five clipped, downward 'here's. I avoided the 'birdie birdie' and 'cheer cheer' mnemonics I know, though 'here' sounds close to 'cheer'.
items.elements: Two long, slow upward slurs from about 1.8 to 3.2 kHz (0.2-0.6 s and 0.95-1.45 s). Then five short, evenly spaced down-slurs from about 3.5 to 1.8 kHz (1.55-3.0 s), each with a clear harmonic above it.

items.phrase: Oh, where've you been? Where'd you go now, ooooh
items.grounds: I fitted the 1 + 3 + 4 grouping and the long falling tail (the drawn-out 'ooooh') to the picture, but I knew the 'who cooks for you, who cooks for you-all' rhythm beforehand, and the question-like shape of my words comes partly from that.
items.elements: Low hoots around 0.5 kHz with arched harmonics up to 2 kHz: one faint opening hoot near 0.3 s, a group of three (about 0.8, 1.15, 1.4 s), a short gap, a group of four (about 1.9, 2.35, 2.75, 3.05 s), then a drawn-out tail sliding down from about 3.2 to 3.6 s.

items.phrase: Hey, sister, sister, sister, sister, sister, sister, sister, sister, ah
items.grounds: The repeated high-then-low pairs, with the first note of each stressed, called for a repeated two-syllable word stressed on the first syllable, with a weak opener and a closing note; I knew the 'teacher, teacher' mnemonic and picked another word with the same shape, so the trochee itself is not independent of that knowledge.
items.elements: A run of repeated two-note units, each a sharp high stroke near 4.5-5 kHz followed by a lower down-sweep from about 4 to 3 kHz. The first unit near 0.2 s is faint and shows only the low note, then eight full units follow, getting louder up to about 2.7 s, and the song ends with a single lower slurred note near 2.9 s.

items.phrase: Tick, tick, tick, tick, tick, tick, why me? GO!
items.grounds: Six even short notes became six 'tick's, the two rising notes became the question 'why me?', and the loud final drop became a stressed 'GO!'; I knew the 'pleased, pleased, pleased to MEET-cha' mnemonic, and my stress on the last note matches its shape.
items.elements: Six short, evenly spaced notes that jump up to about 6.5 kHz and drop to about 5 kHz (0.25-1.1 s), then two longer notes that dip to about 3 kHz and rise again (about 1.2-1.3 and 1.4-1.55 s), then one loud, emphatic down-slur from about 9 kHz to 2.5 kHz near 1.65 s.

items.phrase: Hey you, fall down, now, tick tick tick tick, CHEER CHEER CHEER CHEER, up?
items.grounds: Each group got its own words from the picture: two rise-falls, two falls, one hooked note, four quick low notes, four loud falling notes, and a rising last note (a question); I knew 'sweet sweet sweet, I'm so sweet' and kept away from it, but 'cheer' for the bright falling notes may be colored by it.
items.elements: Two notes that rise to about 8 kHz and drop, two falling strokes from about 7 to 4 kHz, one hooked note going down to about 3 kHz, four short loud lower notes around 3.5-5 kHz (1.0-1.55 s), four loud notes falling from about 7 to 4 kHz with a hook (1.6-2.2 s), and a final up-slur from 3 to 6 kHz.

items.phrase: Chick! Wheeere's the boss? Is he in? ZIP, gone.
items.grounds: The words follow the picture's order: a click-like opener, a long rising word, the buzzy pair and falling slur as 'the boss', the short rise and low blip as 'is he in', the thin high spike as 'ZIP' and the final drop as 'gone'; I knew that this species is described with mnemonics like 'quick, pick up the beer check', which probably pushed me toward a sharp 'Chick!' opener.
items.elements: A sharp broadband chip near 0.27 s; a long slur rising from about 1.8 to 3.5 kHz that ends in a quick drop (0.5-0.72 s); a buzzy burst of two harsh notes around 0.9-1.05 s; a falling slur from 3 to 2 kHz; a short note that rises then falls near 1.3 s; a low blip; a thin high spike up to 10 kHz near 1.5 s; and a final down-stroke from 4 to 2 kHz. There is a faint tail near 1.75 s that may be background.

items.phrase: Moan, tap tap tap tap tap, fall-and-shiver
items.species: Eastern Towhee (the label given to me, not my own identification)
items.grounds: The low drooping note became 'moan', the five short identical marks became five 'tap's, and the downward slide into a buzzy trill became 'fall-and-shiver'. I know the usual 'drink-your-tea' mnemonic for this species, but I left it out because this cut has five short middle notes, not one or two.
items.elements: One low, longer note dipping from about 4 to 3 kHz (0.25-0.5 s), then five short, evenly spaced chevron notes near 3.7 kHz (0.6-1.15 s), then a steep slide down from about 8 to 5 kHz that runs straight into a pulsed trill near 4.7 kHz (1.3-1.8 s). Faint background pulses near 5 kHz run through the whole cut.

items.phrase: Faaar, high, then low
items.species: White-throated Sparrow (the label given to me)
items.grounds: Four long, pure, held notes, the first the longest and the last three stepping down in pitch, so I chose four slow single-syllable words that fall when spoken. I know 'Old Sam Peabody' and 'Oh sweet Canada' for this species, but neither fits this falling, untrilled shape, so I used neither.
items.elements: A long, faint, steady whistle near 4.4 kHz that sinks slightly over 0-2.1 s, then three cleaner held whistles that step down: about 4.5 kHz (2.2-3.0 s), 4.0 kHz (3.1-3.7 s) and 3.2 kHz (3.75-4.85 s). Scattered chips from other birds sit in the background.

items.phrase: Hi there
items.species: Black-capped Chickadee (the label given to me)
items.grounds: Two sustained notes, the second lower and a little longer, read like a two-word greeting whose second word drops. My knowledge of the 'fee-bee' song probably made me expect two notes and lean toward a greeting, though the picture shows the two notes plainly.
items.elements: Two clean whistles: a higher one near 3.9 kHz that drops slightly to 3.6 kHz (0.23-0.63 s), then after a short gap a lower, level one near 3.1-3.2 kHz (0.73-1.2 s).

items.phrase: Buzz, WHEE!
items.species: Alder Flycatcher (the label given to me)
items.grounds: The wide, noisy first block is buzz-like and the tall, steep, loud second stroke is a sharp exclaimed rise, so 'buzz' then a stressed 'WHEE'. Treating only the loud part as the song, and the arcs as something else, comes partly from what I already know of this species' short two-part song ('free-beer'); I did not use those words.
items.elements: Two faint rise-and-fall arcs (0.15-0.5 s and 0.6-1.0 s, about 2.5 to 6.5 to 3 kHz), probably a fainter call or another bird. Then the loud main song: a broad buzzy burst at 3-4 kHz rising a little (1.28-1.55 s), followed by a sharp, steep up-and-down note reaching very high (1.62-1.85 s).

items.phrase: Up? Up? Drop drop drop drop drop
items.species: Northern Cardinal (the label given to me)
items.grounds: Two long rising sweeps became two questioning 'Up?'s, and five short falling strokes became five clipped 'drop's. I know this species' 'what-cheer' and 'birdie birdie' mnemonics and avoided them, though knowing them may have shaped the rise-then-repeat framing.
items.elements: Two long upslurs rising from about 1.8 to 3.2 kHz (0.2-0.6 s and 0.9-1.45 s), then five short, quick downslurs falling from about 3.5 to 1.7 kHz, evenly spaced from 1.58 to 2.97 s.

items.phrase: who cooks for you, who cooks for you all
items.grounds: The picture shows a group of four, then a group of four more, then a long falling tail, and that suggested a 4 + 5 phrase whose last word is drawn out and drops. To be honest, these exact words are a mnemonic I already knew for a low hooting owl. They came from memory, and the picture only seemed to confirm them.
items.elements: Very low hooting notes, with the strongest energy near 0.5 kHz and stacked harmonics. Each note is a rise-and-fall arch. There is a faint short upsweep at 0.3 s, then arched hoots at about 0.8, 1.15, 1.4, 1.9, 2.4, 2.8 and 3.05 s, and the song ends in a sliding downward slur around 3.3-3.5 s.

items.phrase: oh dear me
items.grounds: I chose three long sustained words, each lower than the last, with the final one longest, to match the three level whistles stepping down. The words themselves are a sparrow mnemonic I already knew; they did not come from the picture alone.
items.elements: A long, thin, steady whistle near 4.4 kHz runs from 0 to 1.7 s, falling very slightly. It may come from a second bird. After a burst at 2.2 s come three clean level whistles that step down in pitch: about 4.5 kHz (2.3-2.95 s), 4.0 kHz (3.1-3.6 s) and 3.2 kHz (3.8-4.8 s). Faint short downslurs from other birds are scattered through the cut.

items.phrase: chew chew chew chew chew chew, why? why? down!
items.grounds: Every word comes from the shapes in the picture: short falling words for the six falling chips, 'why?' with its rising question tone for the two dip-and-rise notes, and a long, stressed, falling 'down!' for the final big sweep. None of the words came from prior knowledge.
items.elements: Six quick, sharp downslurred notes, each falling from about 6.5 to 4.5 kHz, come at about 0.22-1.05 s. The later ones have high overtone-like strokes up to about 9 kHz. Next come two V-shaped notes that dip to about 3 kHz and climb back to 6.5 kHz (1.15-1.35 s and 1.4-1.55 s). The song ends with one long, loud downsweep from 9 to 2.5 kHz (1.6-1.75 s).

items.phrase: here, dear
items.grounds: I wanted two long single-syllable vowels, the second lower and a little longer, to match the two level whistles. I deliberately avoided the well-known mnemonic for this pattern ('hey, sweetie'), though knowing that pattern shaped my sense of the song.
items.elements: Two clear, nearly level whistles separated by a short gap. The first is higher, about 3.9 kHz easing down to 3.6 kHz (0.23-0.63 s). The second is lower and slightly longer, about 3.1-3.2 kHz (0.73-1.2 s).

items.phrase: Tick! Climb up! tick, tick, sliding, flip, bop, zing, drop, oh.
items.grounds: I gave one word to each element, matched to its shape: 'tick' for each click, a rising 'climb up!' for the long upsweep, a two-syllable falling 'sliding' for the descending glide, short words for the flicks and blips, 'zing' for the high upsweep, 'drop' for the downstroke and a soft 'oh' for the faint end. None of the words came from prior knowledge.
items.elements:
A busy, varied phrase:
- a broadband click or buzz at 0.27 s
- a long rising sweep from 1.7 to 4.5 kHz that snaps down at 0.5-0.75 s
- two broadband clicks at about 0.9 and 1.0 s
- a descending glide from 3 to 1.8 kHz at 1.03-1.25 s
- a quick up-and-down flick at 1.27-1.38 s
- a short low blip at 1.43 s
- a steep upsweep to about 10 kHz at 1.5 s
- a sharp downstroke at 1.57 s
- a faint final note at 1.75 s

items.phrase: Well, tick tick tick tick tick, wheeze.
items.grounds: A soft opening word for the low slurred note, five identical one-syllable clicks for the five clipped notes, and one long falling-then-held word for the swoop into the buzz; all of it came from the picture and none from anything I already knew.
items.elements: One longish low note around 3-4 kHz that slurs down (0.27-0.5 s), then five short, evenly spaced clipped notes with a vertical stroke and a small flat tick at about 3.7 kHz (0.6-1.2 s), then a steep drop from about 9 to 5 kHz that runs straight into a long, finely pulsed buzz held at about 4.7 kHz (1.3-1.8 s).

items.phrase: And cheaper cheaper cheaper cheaper cheaper cheaper cheaper cheaper, oh.
items.grounds: The picture shows eight two-part units, each with a longer, stressed first part and a short second part, so I used a two-syllable word stressed on the first syllable, repeated eight times, with one small word at each end; honestly, reading it as repeated two-syllable pairs that get louder was primed by knowing the well-known 'teacher teacher' song, and I chose 'cheaper' on purpose to avoid that stock word.
items.elements: A series of paired notes that gets louder: each pair is a high stroke falling from about 7 to 4.5 kHz with a short flat tail, then a sharper note dipping to about 3 kHz. There is one partial note at the start, eight full pairs, and a final low slur that dips to 2 kHz and rises to 3.6 kHz.

items.phrase: So up, hi, down; up, hi, down, crash, whip!
items.grounds: Each arc's rise, high blip and fall became 'up, hi, down' said twice, the cut-off falling note at the start became 'so', and the noisy broadband ending became 'crash' then a short 'whip'; all from the picture.
items.elements: A falling note cut off at the start, then two matching arcs. Each arc is a slur rising from about 2.6 to 4.3 kHz, a tiny high blip near 6.3 kHz, and a slur falling from about 5.5 to 2.8 kHz. The song ends with a loud, harsh, broadband buzz at about 3-4 kHz with sweeps reaching up to 10 kHz, then a quick up-and-down stroke.

items.phrase: Peek peek, fall fall, sink sink, tick tick tick tick, cheer cheer cheer cheery.
items.grounds: I used one one-syllable word per note, changing the word with each group as the notes went from rising, to falling, to low clipped checks, to loud falling strokes, and I gave the last note two syllables for its upturn; all from the picture.
items.elements: Fourteen sharp notes in four groups: two notes that shoot up to about 8 kHz and drop back, two strokes falling from 7 to 4 kHz, two smaller, lower notes, four short loud checkmark notes around 3-5 kHz, and finally four loud strokes falling from 7 to about 3.5 kHz, the last one ending in an upturn.

items.phrase: Why? Whyyy? Drop, drop, drop, drop, drop.
items.grounds: The two long rising slurs sounded to me like drawn-out questions, and the five quick falling notes like five clipped words that drop in pitch; the words came from the picture, though I recognized the pattern as resembling a cardinal before writing them and deliberately avoided the familiar 'cheer' mnemonic.
items.elements: Two long, slow slurs rising from about 1.8 to 3.2 kHz (the second one longer), followed by five short, evenly spaced, sharp notes falling from about 3.5 to 1.7 kHz.

items.phrase: so, who knew you'd move through to-o-o
items.grounds: One short soft syllable for the faint lead-in, then six low, round 'oo' words of even length for the arched hoots, with the last one stretched to follow the falling tail; the 'oo' vowel sound came from how low and hollow the harmonic arches look, not from any bird I know.
items.elements: Very low song (about 0.5 kHz with stacked harmonics up to 2 kHz): a faint short lead-in near 0.3 s, then six arched, hooting notes of about equal length (about 0.8 to 3.1 s), with the last one sliding down into a falling tail around 3.3 to 3.6 s.

items.phrase: a PICK-up PICK-up PICK-up PICK-up PICK-up PICK-up PICK-up PICK-up, then
items.grounds: The picture shows eight strong-weak pairs, the first part high and sharp and the second lower, growing louder, with one pickup note and one closing note, so I wrote a two-syllable word stressed on the first syllable, eight times; to be honest, I recognised the pattern as the known 'teacher-teacher' mnemonic and deliberately avoided that word, but that knowledge probably shaped my choice of a stress-first two-beat word.
items.elements: A two-part unit repeated eight times, getting louder and higher: a sharp high downslur (about 7 down to 4.5 kHz) followed by a lower V-shaped downsweep (about 4 down to 2.5 kHz). There is one lone low note at the start and a buzzy lower note at the end (about 2.9 s).

items.phrase: so, here we go, here we go, buzz zip zing zap
items.grounds: 'so' is the first falling note; each 'here we go' follows one rise-tick-fall figure, with 'go' drawn out for the long descent; the four harsh one-syllable words match the dark, buzzy, steeply swept ending, and all of it came from the picture, not from any knowledge of a species.
items.elements: An opening falling note, then two identical three-part figures (a rising slur from about 2.6 to 4.3 kHz, a short high tick near 6.3 kHz, a long descent from 5.5 to 2.8 kHz). After a gap comes a louder, harsher ending (1.3 to 1.85 s): a buzz near 3.5 kHz, a very steep upsweep to about 10 kHz, a rising slur, and a sharp drop.

items.phrase: Why? Whyyy? Down, down, down, down, down.
items.grounds: The two long rising slurs look like a voice rising on a question, with the second one stretched longer, and the five quick sharp downstrokes look like a word stressed hard at the start that drops, so the words follow the shapes directly; none came from knowledge of a bird.
items.elements: Two long, slow rising slurs (about 1.8 up to 3.2 kHz; the second is longer, about 0.5 s), followed by five short, evenly spaced, loud downslurs (about 3.5 down to 1.7 kHz), each with a faint harmonic above.

items.phrase: Tick. Sli-i-ide up SNAP! chk chk, sigh, dip, flip, bump, ZIP, drop.
items.grounds: Each word stands for one mark in the order they come: a long stretched 'slide up' for the long rising slur, 'snap' for its sharp peak, clicky words for the broadband ticks, a falling 'sigh', and a stressed 'ZIP' for the tall high upsweep; it all came from the picture, though the count is uncertain because the cut is noisy.
items.elements: A busy, irregular song: a broadband click (about 0.27 s), a long rising slur (1.7 to 3.2 kHz) that ends in a sharp peak-and-drop, two broadband ticks (about 0.9 to 1.0 s), a falling note near 2.8 kHz, a low dip, a quick rise-and-fall hook near 4 kHz, a short low note, a very high upsweep (about 1.5 s), and a final sharp downstroke. Background noise is heavy.

items.phrase: Oh, pick pick pick pick pick, whee-rattle
items.grounds: The long low first note became 'Oh', the five even clipped notes became five 'pick's, and the high falling sweep followed by the pulsed buzz became 'whee-rattle'; all of it came from the picture, nothing from what I already knew.
items.elements: A low, slightly drooping note (0.25-0.5 s, about 3 kHz), then five short identical hooked notes near 3.7 kHz, then a fast steep sweep falling from about 8 to 5 kHz that runs straight into a buzzy rattle of about ten pulses (1.42-1.75 s). Faint repeated notes from another bird sit near 5 kHz in the background.

items.phrase: Here, there, gone
items.grounds: Three long, level, one-syllable words that can be said on falling pitches match the three held whistles stepping down; I noticed the stepping-down shape is like the tune of 'Three Blind Mice', but I deliberately did not use those words.
items.elements: Three loud, steady, pure whistles, each about half a second to a second long, stepping down in pitch (about 4.5, 4.0 and 3.2 kHz, from 2.3 to 4.8 s), with scattered short downstrokes around them. A long faint level tone near 4.3 kHz over the first two seconds may be the same bird or a background one, so I did not count it.

items.phrase: Dew dew dew dew dew dew, tea, sweet, sweet, cheer
items.grounds: Six quick falling notes became six 'dew's, the single higher note became 'tea', the two dip-and-rise notes became two rising 'sweet's, and the big final fall became a stressed, drawn-out 'cheer'; all of it came from the shapes in the picture.
items.elements: Six short notes slurring down from about 6.5 to 4.5 kHz, then one higher falling note, then two V-shaped notes that dip to 3 kHz and climb back to 6.5 kHz, then one loud long sweep falling from about 9 to 2.5 kHz to end.

items.phrase: Here... now
items.grounds: Two long held one-syllable words, the first said higher and the second lower, fit the two whistles; I recognised the shape as the familiar two-note 'fee-bee' type of song and avoided those words on purpose, so the words are mine but that recognition was there.
items.elements: Two long pure whistles: the first about 0.4 s long at about 3.9 kHz, easing down slightly; then, after a short gap, a lower one about 0.45 s long at about 3.1 kHz.

items.phrase: Whee whee, see see, tick tick, chip chip chip chip, cheer cheer cheer cheer, rise
items.grounds: Each group of like notes got a repeated one-syllable word matching its pitch and shape: high rise-and-fall 'whee', falling 'see', faint 'tick', low hooked 'chip', loud falling 'cheer', and 'rise' for the last upward note; all of it came from the picture.
items.elements: A run of short, sharply bent notes: two high notes that rise and fall (up to about 8 kHz), two falling notes from 7 to 4 kHz, two small fainter notes, four lower hooked notes at 4-5 kHz, then four loud falling notes from 7 to 4 kHz with a hook at the end, and a final rising note.
